This is a '''list of banks in Canada''', including chartered banks, [[credit union]]s, [[Trust company#Banking services|trusts]], and other [[financial services]] companies that offer banking services and may be popularly referred to as "banks".

== Largest banks ==

=== Big Five ===
The top five Canadian banks are collectively referred to as the "Big Five" due to their dominant position and significant influence within the country's banking and financial industry. This term has been used for many years to characterize these major banks, and it highlights their substantial market share and impact on Canada's economy. The financial sector of Canada is especially concentrated in these banks, which has been seen as a result of [[protectionist]] policies of the government and the country's small and dispersed population. These banks grew at an extraordinary rate of 10.7 percent per year, on average, from 2008 to 2018 compared with 3.64 percent for the five largest U.S. banks.<ref name="Financial Post 1970">{{cite news |last=Pelletier |first=Martin |date=30 Jul 2018 |title=Our nation of oligopolies not good for consumers, but great for investors |website=Financial Post |url=https://financialpost.com/investing/how-canadas-oligopolies-have-been-big-winners-for-investors |access-date=12 Dec 2020}}</ref> While most Canadian banks operate only within Canada, the Big Five are best described as Canadian multinational financial [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerates]] that each have a large Canadian banking division.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Big Five Banks in Canada |url=https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/bigfivebanks.asp |access-date=4 Jan 2020 |website=Investopedia}}</ref>

=== Big Six ===
[[National Bank of Canada]], which began as a regional bank in [[Quebec]] but expanded nationally, is the sixth largest Canadian bank.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Are the Big Six Banks in Canada Today? |url=https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/bigsixbanks.asp |access-date=30 Dec 2023 |website=Investopedia |language=en}}</ref> In 2025 it took over the [[Canadian Western Bank]]. In 2022, Canada’s Big Six held about 93% of all banking assets in the country. It is the same share they held a decade earlier, and a decade before that.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=How big banks dominate Canada's financial landscape - National {{!}} Globalnews.ca |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/9634933/canada-big-banks-analysis/ |access-date=30 Dec 2023 |website=Global News |language=ken-US}}</ref> [[Royal Bank of Canada|RBC]]’s $13.5-billion takeover of [[HSBC Bank Canada|HSBC’s Canadian division]], announced in November 2022, gave it around $134 billion in HSBC assets<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 Nov 2022 |title=Royal Bank of Canada signs deal to buy HSBC Canada for $13.5B |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/business/article/royal-bank-of-canada-signs-deal-to-buy-hsbc-canada-for-135b/ |access-date=30 Dec 2023 |website=CTVNews |language=en}}</ref> and increased the 93% share of assets the Big Six have to almost 95%.<ref name=":1" />

== Importance of Canada's financial institutions ==

=== Domestic systemically important bank (D-SIB) ===
A domestic systemically important bank (D-SIB) is a bank that could disrupt the domestic economy should it fail. Canada's Big Six are designated as D-SIBs. D-SIBs are so important to the functioning of the financial system and the economy, that they cannot be wound up under a conventional bankruptcy and liquidation process should they fail. The failure of any one of Canada’s D-SIBs, with the potential loss of financial services, even for a short period of time, could have a serious impact on Canada’s economy.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Large Banks (D-SIBs) |url=https://www.cdic.ca/what-happens-in-a-failure/resolution-of-large-banks/large-banks-d-sibs/ |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=cdic.ca |language=en}}</ref>

=== Desjardins ===
The [[Autorité des marchés financiers (Quebec)|Autorité des marchés financiers]], which oversees Quebec’s financial sector, designated [[Desjardins Group]] as a D-SIB.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Notice related to designation of Desjardins Group as a domestic systemically important financial institution |url=https://lautorite.qc.ca/fileadmin/lautorite/reglementation/assurances-inst-depot/avis-ifis-d-cq_desjardins_a.pdf |access-date=2024-01-25}}</ref>

=== Global systemically important bank (G-SIB) ===
A global systemically important bank is a bank whose systemic risk profile is deemed to be of such importance that the bank’s failure would trigger a wider financial crisis and threaten the global economy. The [[Basel Committee on Banking Supervision|Basel Committee]] has developed a formula for determining which banks are G-SIBs, deploying criteria including size, interconnectedness and complexity. National regulators subject banks determined to be G-SIBs to stricter prudential regulation such as higher capital requirements and extra surcharges, or more stringent stress tests.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Global systemically important bank (G-Sib) definition - Risk.net |url=https://www.risk.net/definition/global-systemically-important-bank-g-sib |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=www.risk.net |language=en}}</ref>

In Canada, the [[Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions]] designated [[Royal Bank of Canada]] and [[Toronto-Dominion Bank]] as G-SIBs as well as D-SIBs.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-11-27 |title=2023 List of Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) |url=https://www.fsb.org/2023/11/2023-list-of-global-systemically-important-banks-g-sibs/ |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=www.fsb.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2" />

=== Digital banking and fintech trends ===
In recent years, Canada has experienced a steady shift toward digital banking services, driven by changing consumer preferences and technological innovation. A growing share of Canadians now use digital-only banking platforms for at least part of their financial activities, reflecting increased demand for low-cost, mobile-first services.

Established banks have responded by expanding their digital offerings and investing in online infrastructure, while digital-first institutions such as Tangerine Bank and EQ Bank have gained traction through competitive pricing and simplified user experiences.<ref>{{cite web |title=Canada Banking Sector Performance Q1 2026 |url=https://finanque.com/banks |access-date=2026-04-20}}</ref>

This trend is expected to accelerate alongside the development of open banking frameworks in Canada.

==Banks by legal classification==
Banks in Canada are classified by their ownership as domestic banks, subsidiaries of foreign banks, or branches of foreign banks. For a greater explanation of the classifications, see ''[[Banking in Canada]]'' and ''[[Bank Act (Canada)]]''.

===Schedule I banks (domestic banks)===
Under the [[Bank_Act_(Canada)|Bank Act]], Schedule I are banks that are not a subsidiary of a foreign bank, even if they have foreign shareholders. == Credit unions ==
[[File:Saskatoon Credit Union.jpg|thumb|Branch of Affinity Credit Union in [[Saskatoon, Saskatchewan]].]]
[[File:Tower of Complexe Desjardins 2005-10-22.JPG|thumb|The executive headquarters of the [[Desjardins Group]] in Montreal.]]
Canada has a strong [[co-operative]] financial services sector, which consists of [[credit unions]] ([[caisses populaires]] in Quebec and other French speaking regions).  At the end of 2001, Canada's credit union sector consisted of 681 credit unions and 914 ''caisses populaires'', with more than 3,600 locations and 4,100 automated teller machines.<ref name="FinanceCanada2003">{{cite web |url=http://www.fin.gc.ca/toc/2003/ccu_-eng.asp |title=Canada's Credit Unions and Caisses Populaires – March 2003 |publisher=Fin.gc.ca |date=13 Nov 2008 |access-date=13 Aug 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100213150245/http://www.fin.gc.ca/toc/2003/ccu_-eng.asp |archive-date=13 Feb 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> By the end of 2019, consolidation reduced this number to 251 credits unions and caisses populaires outside Quebec, according to the [[Canadian Credit Union Association]] (CCUA).<ref name="CUCA Q4 2020">{{cite web |title=Largest 100 Credit Unions 2021 4Q |url=https://ccua.com/app/uploads/private-files/top100-4Q21_29-Mar-22.pdf |access-date=27 Apr 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ccua.com/credit_unions_in_canada|title=Credit Unions in Canada|date=1 Sep 2019|website=ccua.com|publisher=Canadian Credit Union Association|archive-url=https://archive.today/20190902041845/https://www.ccua.com/credit_unions_in_canada|archive-date=2 September 2019|url-status=live|access-date=2 Sep 2019}}</ref><ref name = "CUCC_Q4_2012">{{cite web |url=http://www.cucentral.ca/FactsFigures/top100-4Q12_19-Mar-13.pdf |title=Largest 100 Credit Unions / Caisses Populaires |publisher=Cucentral.ca |access-date=14 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130626040531/http://www.cucentral.ca/FactsFigures/top100-4Q12_19-Mar-13.pdf |archive-date=26 Jun 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Canada has the world's highest per capita membership in the credit union movement, with over 10 million members, or about one-third of the Canadian population.  While the sector is active in all parts of the country, it is strongest in the western provinces and in Quebec. In Quebec 70 per cent of the population belongs to a caisse populaire, while in Saskatchewan close to 60 per cent belongs to a credit union.
